questions.stem: Which statement is the law of magnetism?

options.text: opposite poles attract; like poles repel
options.explanation: This is the interaction rule between two magnetic poles.

options.text: all poles attract each other
options.explanation: Like poles push apart — attraction is only half the story.

options.text: all poles repel each other
options.explanation: Opposite poles pull together, so total repulsion is wrong.

options.text: poles only interact through contact
options.explanation: Magnetic forces act at a distance through the field.

questions.stem: Where is the magnetic force of a bar magnet strongest?

options.text: only inside the material
options.explanation: The external pull is strongest just outside each pole.

options.text: at the poles
options.explanation: Field lines bunch most densely at the ends.

options.text: at the middle of the bar
options.explanation: The middle is the weakest region of a bar magnet.

options.text: equally everywhere along the bar
options.explanation: Strength varies sharply from poles to middle.

questions.stem: A suspended bar is brought near a magnet and is attracted to BOTH poles in turn. What can be concluded?

options.text: the bar must be a magnet with two north poles
options.explanation: Like poles would repel, not attract.

options.text: the test proves nothing at all
options.explanation: It rules the bar magnetic — just not necessarily a magnet.

options.text: the bar is a magnetic substance but not necessarily a magnet
options.explanation: Either pole attracts unmagnetised magnetic material, so attraction alone is inconclusive.

options.text: the bar must be a magnet with two south poles
options.explanation: No magnet has two like poles; attraction to both points to induced magnetism.

questions.stem: Which observation would PROVE that an object is a magnet?

options.text: it is attracted to a known magnet
options.explanation: Magnetic substances are attracted too — attraction is ambiguous.

options.text: it is made of iron
options.explanation: Iron objects need not be magnetised.

options.text: it sticks to a wall
options.explanation: Sticking depends on the wall, not on magnetism alone.

options.text: it repels the north pole of a known magnet
options.explanation: Only another magnet can repel a pole, so repulsion is conclusive.

questions.stem: Two bar magnets are placed with their south poles facing. What happens?

options.text: they repel each other
options.explanation: Like poles repel under the law of magnetism.

options.text: they attract each other
options.explanation: Attraction needs opposite poles facing.

options.text: nothing, because the poles are the same
options.explanation: Matching poles interact most strongly — by repelling.

options.text: the magnets lose their magnetism
options.explanation: Bring poles together does not demagnetise them here.

questions.modelAnswer: Opposite poles attract each other and like poles repel each other.

questions.stem: State the only interaction that proves an object is a magnet.
questions.modelAnswer: Repulsion by a known magnet, because magnetic substances are only ever attracted.

questions.stem: Explain why attraction to a magnet is not a certain test for magnetism.
questions.modelAnswer: A magnet attracts both opposite poles and unmagnetised magnetic substances, so an attracted object could simply be iron or steel that has had magnetism induced in it. Repulsion, by contrast, can only come from a second magnet with its like pole facing, so only repulsion separates a magnet from an ordinary magnetic material.

questions.stem: Two labelled bars, X and Y, hang freely. When the north pole of a strong magnet is brought near X's end, X swings away; near Y's end it swings in. Identify what each bar is.
questions.modelAnswer: X repels the north pole, so X must itself be a magnet with a north pole facing out. Y is attracted, so Y is a magnetic material — or a magnet with a south pole out — but the attraction alone does not decide which.

questions.stem: Which list contains only magnetic substances?

options.text: nickel, plastic, iron, glass
options.explanation: Plastic and glass are non-magnetic materials.

options.text: iron, steel, cobalt, nickel
options.explanation: These are the magnetic metals of the course.

options.text: copper, iron, nickel, zinc
options.explanation: Copper and zinc are not magnetic substances.

options.text: steel, aluminium, cobalt, tin
options.explanation: Aluminium and tin are non-magnetic.

questions.stem: Which material is used for a permanent magnet?

options.text: copper wire
options.explanation: Copper is not a magnetic substance.

options.text: aluminium alloy
options.explanation: Aluminium does not hold induced magnetism.

options.text: magnetically hard steel
options.explanation: Hard materials retain magnetisation, which is what permanence requires.

options.text: magnetically soft pure iron
options.explanation: Soft iron demagnetises easily — the temporary choice.

questions.stem: Why is soft iron chosen as the core of an electromagnet?

options.text: it keeps its magnetism permanently, strengthening the electromagnet
options.explanation: Permanent retention is the failure mode here, not the goal.

options.text: soft iron conducts the electric current round the circuit
options.explanation: The coil, not the core, carries the current.

options.text: soft iron is the cheapest metal available
options.explanation: The choice is magnetic behaviour, not price.

options.text: it magnetises and demagnetises readily, so the magnet switches with the current
options.explanation: Soft-iron magnetism follows the field on and off.

questions.stem: A steel pin hangs near an electromagnet. When the current is switched on the pin swings towards it; when switched off it drops. What has happened to the pin?

options.text: magnetism was induced in it while the field was present
options.explanation: The field induces magnetism in the steel, attracting it; removal lets it drop.

options.text: the pin melted slightly and lost rigidity
options.explanation: No heating is involved in the switching behaviour.

options.text: the current pushed the pin with an electric force
options.explanation: The pin is not part of the circuit; the pull is magnetic.

options.text: the pin was already a permanent magnet
options.explanation: A permanent magnet would be attracted whether or not the current flowed.

questions.stem: Which statement about induced magnetism is correct?

options.text: induction works on any metal
options.explanation: Only magnetic substances can be induced.

options.text: the induced material is always attracted to the inducing magnet
options.explanation: Induction always places an unlike pole nearest the magnet.

options.text: the induced material may repel the inducing magnet
options.explanation: Only two magnets can repel; induced poles attract.

options.text: induction only works on already-magnetised objects
options.explanation: Induction magnetises unmagnetised magnetic materials.

questions.stem: Name the two classes of magnetic material according to how long they keep their magnetism.
questions.modelAnswer: Magnetically hard materials, which keep their magnetism, and magnetically soft materials, which lose it easily.

questions.stem: Give two magnetic elements used to make magnetic alloys.
questions.modelAnswer: Any two of iron, cobalt and nickel — for example iron and nickel.

questions.stem: Explain why a paperclip chain can hang from a magnet, with each clip holding the next.
questions.modelAnswer: The magnet induces magnetism in the first clip, giving it poles of its own; that induced clip then acts as the inducing magnet for the second clip, and so on down the chain. Each clip is attracted because its nearest induced pole is always unlike the pole above it, so the whole chain hangs together while the field is present.

questions.stem: A scrapyard crane needs to pick up and release steel car bodies on demand. Choose the magnet design and justify it using hard and soft magnetic behaviour.
questions.modelAnswer: The crane uses an electromagnet: a coil around a soft iron core. The soft core magnetises strongly while current flows, grabbing the steel bodies, and demagnetises the instant the current stops, releasing them. A permanent hard-steel magnet could not let go of the load on command.
